verdict.reasoning: Patient: "I would say maybe about two months or so, I've been feeling like this" and "I just get really nervous every morning about leaving the house, and it's started to really worry me" and "I just really dread, going there" (work).

Patient describes difficulty sleeping: "I can't get to sleep for hours and hours and hours" and "Not for ages, I'm, I'm lying awake all night" and estimates only "maybe, three, four hours" of shallow sleep.
Patient reports heart racing: "my heart kind of racing" and "just a constant like, rapid heart beating" and discusses duration and characteristics with doctor, consistent with palpitations.

Patient: "I would say maybe about two months or so... and that probably coincides with, me starting a new job" and "I work for a, a, a fashion retailer, in um, the head office team" and "it's been really stressful" and "my boss is not very nice to me."

Bedtime: Doctor: "What time do you go to bed?" Patient: "About ten, eleven, probably." Sleep latency and quality: "I can't get to sleep for hours and hours and hours" and "even when I'm in sleep it's such a shallow sleep."

Patient: "I find my, my heart kind of racing, and then I'm just like panicking that I'm gonna be late" and "I wake up in a panic thinking I am gonna be late so, it's just kind of like, just a constant like, rapid heart beating."

Doctor asks: "Does it feel like a regular fast beat, or an irregular, beat?" Patient: "Irregular, I think." Duration: "it can be anything, I think couple of minutes, or the other day... lying there... for like ten minutes." Described as rapid heart beating.

Low energy/anhedonia: "It's just, really, really low" energy, "I find no enjoyment at all" and "anything that, previously was, really fun is just not, it's not enjoyable" and she is "on edge the whole time."

Social withdrawal: "sometimes... I know that I'm not gonna have fun, because I don't want to, go out and, do things that I would normally have done." Activities: "I did used to like to like go running, and... play tennis... but now it's just not, I'm just not enjoying it, I'm not... going out to do that quite so much."
Patient: "I find public transport really stressful anyway, especially being on the tube it's, 'cause it's quite, getting warmer so it's just really airless."
Attendance: Doctor: "have you... had to miss work?" Patient: "No" but adds "pretty much every morning I think, ohh I should call in sick or like, just not go."

Low mood: "I'm pretty much, down like, I don't enjoy... my day at all" and "even at the weekends... constant, feeling of just being a bit, down, a bit unhappy." Suicidal ideation: "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts or any, thoughts that have been that extreme."
Support: "I have a good support system, like I do have good family and stuff."

Eating: Doctor: "You're eating regularly otherwise?" Patient: "Yeah" and "Probably, not, significant changes maybe... I wouldn't say that I'm eating like, much differently. Ohh that, I probably have more chocolate than normal."
Doctor: "Before this did you have any similar times in your life when you felt like this?" Patient: "Not really I, I'm, no, I would say... I've never felt, anything this bad before."
Patient: "I talk to my mum, because she also suffers from, well she's, suffered from like depression in the past."
Doctor: "Who do you live with at home?" Patient: "Yeah, I live with my parents, just my parents."

Alcohol: "probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday... I probably go over my limit just on those days" and "maybe a glass of wine during the week" offered by parents; this is consistent with binge-type drinking on weekends and weekday wine.
Smoking: Doctor: "Do you smoke or take any other drugs, or anything?" Patient: "Um, I try not to smoke, but I do, occasionally."
Drugs: same exchange, Patient: "but I don't take drugs."

Openness to therapy: Doctor: "would you be happy to, have, some one-to-one therapy?" Patient: "Yeah I think, yeah I think so." She also says her mum "recommended that I come to the GP" and she has discussed her symptoms with her mum.

Work-related anxiety and depressive symptoms: anxiety linked to job, low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, social/activities reduction. Functional impact: difficulty going to work, low energy, reduced hobbies. No suicidal ideation: "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts."

Anxiety clearly precedes and is tied to work stress and palpitations; insomnia is described in the context of worry about work. Doctor frames anxiety as main problem and later mentions sleep advice; inferring insomnia secondary to anxiety is a direct clinical inference from transcript.

New ~2 months: palpitations "only in the past... couple of months"; doctor: "it is most likely to be... associated with anxiety"; perceived irregular and painful when fast; patient denies typical chest pain: "No, um, well yeah it's painful... when my heart is beating fast but..." implying no separate chest pain complaint.
Doctor: "you can self-refer via the NHS, for what we call like, talking therapy..." and "So I can send you the link for that." Talking therapy is described as inter-behavioural/CBT-type approach.
Doctor: "There are some online resources that are really helpful. Um, can put the details, on there and you can, get on with them straight away."

Doctor: "if you're feeling like it's not helping at all, or your anxiety is getting worse, to the point where you can't cope with work, or you can't, just do your normal things day-to-day. Then, it's important... to give us a call, back and just discuss that, further."
Doctor: "some people, with anxiety they, do need to take medication... but that's, not something that we'd suggest in the first instance." No medication is prescribed in the transcript.
Doctor: "I'll put some more information on your notes about, helping with your, sleep patterns and things like that." This is consistent with sleep hygiene guidance/resources.

Doctor: "it's probably worth having couple of basic blood tests just to make sure that, there's not something triggering that off" (palpitations) and "So if you call the support line you can arrange the, to have the blood test done."
Doctor: "arranging a GP follow-up a week after you've had the tests, so we can just go through the results with you."

Doctor comments on distress: "I can see that you're quite distressed"; the entire content of consultation describes anxiety; thus describing her appearance on mental status as distressed and anxious is supported.
